chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Kutuzov fell back toward Vienna, destroying the bridges over the River Inn at Braunau and the River Traun near Linz as he went. On October 23, the Russian troops were crossing the River Enns. By midday, the Russian baggage train, artillery, and columns of troops were filing through the town of Enns on both sides of the bridge.

It was a warm, rainy autumn day. The wide landscape that opened out below the heights where the Russian batteries guarded the bridge was sometimes veiled by a sheer curtain of slanting rain, and then suddenly revealed in sunlight, with far-off objects glittering as if freshly varnished. Down below, the little town could be seen with its white, red-roofed houses, its cathedral, and its bridge, on both sides of which masses of Russian troops were streaming and jostling. At the bend of the Danube, boats, an island, and a castle with a park stood visible, surrounded by the waters where the Enns flowed into the Danube. The rocky left bank of the Danube was covered with pine forests, with a mysterious backdrop of green treetops and bluish ravines. The towers of a convent rose beyond a stretch of untouched pine forest, and far away on the other side of the Enns, enemy cavalry patrols could be spotted.

On the brow of the hill, among the field guns, the general commanding the rearguard stood with a staff officer, scanning the countryside through his field glass. A little behind them sat Nesvitsky, who had been sent to the rearguard by the commander in chief, perched on the trail of a gun carriage. A Cossack who accompanied him had handed over a knapsack and flask, and Nesvitsky was treating some officers to pies and genuine doppelkümmel liqueur. The officers had gathered around him gladly, some on their knees, others squatting cross-legged on the wet grass.
"Yes, the Austrian prince who built that castle was no fool. Lovely place! Why aren't you eating, gentlemen?" Nesvitsky was saying.

"Thank you very much, Prince," answered one of the officers, pleased to be chatting with such an important staff officer. "It really is a lovely place! We passed right by the park and spotted two deer... and what a magnificent house!"

"Look, Prince," said another officer, who would have loved to take another pie but felt too self-conscious and so pretended to be studying the landscape. "See—our infantry have already made it over there. Look, in the meadow behind the village, three of them are dragging something. They'll clean out that castle," he observed with obvious approval.
"I'm sure they will," said Nesvitsky. "No, but what I'd really love," he added, munching a pie with his moist-lipped, handsome mouth, "would be to slip in over there."
He pointed with a grin toward a turreted convent, his eyes narrowing and gleaming.
"Now that would be something, gentlemen!"
The officers laughed.
"Just to ruffle the nuns a bit. I hear there are Italian girls among them. I swear I'd give five years of my life for it!"
"They must be pretty bored too," said one of the bolder officers with a laugh.
Meanwhile, the staff officer up front pointed something out to the general, who looked through his field glass.

"Yes, that's right, that's right," the general said irritably, lowering his field glass and shrugging. "That's right! They'll come under fire at the crossing. And why are they dragging their feet over there?"

On the far side, the enemy was visible to the naked eye, and a milky-white cloud of smoke rose from their battery. Then came the distant boom of a shot, and the Russian troops could be seen rushing toward the crossing.
Nesvitsky heaved himself up, puffing, and walked over to the general with a smile.
"Wouldn't your excellency care for a little refreshment?" he offered.
"It's a bad business," the general replied without acknowledging the offer. "Our men have wasted too much time."
"Shall I ride over there, your excellency?" Nesvitsky asked.

"Yes, please do," the general answered, and repeated the detailed order that had already been given once before: "And tell the hussars they are to cross last and set fire to the bridge, as I ordered. And the inflammable material on the bridge needs to be inspected again."
"Very good," Nesvitsky replied.
He called over the Cossack with his horse, told him to stow the knapsack and flask, and swung his heavy frame easily into the saddle.
"I really will stop by the convent," he told the officers, who watched him with smiles, and he rode off down the winding path along the hillside.
"Now then, Captain, let's see how far it'll carry. Give it a try!" said the general, turning to an artillery officer. "A bit of fun to pass the time."
"Crew, to your guns!" the officer commanded.
In a moment the men came running cheerfully from their campfires and began loading.
"Fire!" came the command.

Number one jumped nimbly aside. The gun roared with a deafening metallic blast, and a whistling shell flew over the heads of the troops below the hill before landing well short of the enemy, a small puff of smoke marking where it burst.

The faces of officers and soldiers alike brightened at the sound. Everyone stood up and began watching the movements of the Russian troops below—as clearly visible as if they were only a stone's throw away—and the approaching enemy further off. At that same moment, the sun broke fully through the clouds, and the sharp crack of the solitary shot merged with the brilliance of the bright sunshine into one joyful, exhilarating impression.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Two enemy shells had already flown across the bridge, where a crush of men was building up. Halfway across, Prince Nesvitsky had dismounted and now found his bulky body jammed against the railings. He glanced back, laughing, at the Cossack standing a few steps behind him holding two horses by their bridles. Every time Nesvitsky tried to push forward, soldiers and carts shoved him back against the railings, and all he could do was smile.

"Some friend you are!" the Cossack said to a supply wagon driver who was pressing into the infantrymen crowded around his wheels and horses. "What kind of fellow are you? Can't you wait a moment? Don't you see the general needs to get through?"

But the wagon driver paid no attention to the word "general" and shouted at the soldiers blocking his way. "Hey, boys! Keep to the left! Hold up!" But the soldiers, packed shoulder to shoulder with bayonets interlocking, moved across the bridge in a solid mass. Looking over the railing, Prince Nesvitsky watched the quick, noisy little waves of the Enns rippling and swirling around the bridge pilings, chasing one another downstream. Looking at the bridge itself, he saw an equally unbroken living wave of soldiers—shoulder straps, covered shakos, knapsacks, bayonets, long muskets, and beneath the shakos, faces with broad cheekbones, hollow cheeks, and dull, tired expressions—and feet trudging through the sticky mud that coated the bridge planks. Sometimes, through this monotonous stream of men, like a fleck of white foam on the river's current, an officer in a cloak, with a face of a different type, squeezed his way through. Sometimes, like a wood chip spinning in the water, a dismounted hussar, an orderly, or a civilian was carried along in the flood of infantry. And sometimes, like a log drifting downstream, an officers' or company baggage wagon—piled high, covered in leather, and hemmed in on every side—rolled across the bridge.
"It's like a dam burst," said the Cossack, giving up hope. "Are there many more of you coming?"
"A million, all but one!" a wisecracking soldier in a torn coat called back with a wink, and passed on, followed by another—an old man.
"If he"—meaning the enemy—"starts firing at the bridge now," the old soldier said glumly to a comrade, "you'll forget all about scratching yourself."
That soldier moved on, and after him came another riding on a cart.
"Where the hell have the leg wrappings been shoved?" an orderly shouted, running behind the cart and rummaging in the back of it.
He too passed on with the wagon. Then came a group of soldiers who had clearly been drinking.
"And then, old fellow, he smacks him right in the teeth with the butt of his rifle..." a soldier with his greatcoat tucked up tight was saying cheerfully, swinging his arm wide.
"Yeah, and that ham was delicious..." another replied with a loud laugh. And they too moved on, so that Nesvitsky never learned who had been hit in the teeth, or what ham had to do with any of it.
"Bah! Look at them scurry. One cannonball and they think they're all going to die," a sergeant was saying angrily and reproachfully.

"When it flies past me, Papa—the ball, I mean," said a young soldier with an enormous mouth, barely holding back his laughter. "I felt like I was going to die of fright. I really did, honest to God, I was that scared!" he said, as if boasting about having been frightened.

He too passed on. Then came a cart unlike any of the others. It was a German cart pulled by a pair of horses and led by a German, loaded with what looked like an entire household's belongings. A fine brindled cow with a large udder was tied to the back. A woman carrying an infant, an old woman, and a healthy German girl with bright red cheeks sat perched on feather beds. These refugees had evidently been allowed through by special permission. Every soldier's eyes turned toward the women, and as the cart crawled past at walking pace, every remark the soldiers made was about the two younger ones. Each face wore almost the same grin, reflecting thoughts that were anything but proper.
"Look at that—even the German sausage is clearing out!"
"How about selling me the missus?" another soldier called to the German, who strode along angrily and nervously with his eyes fixed on the ground.
"Look how she's dressed herself up! The devils!"
"Hey, Fedotov—they should quarter you with them!"
"I've seen plenty of that before, mate!"
"Where are you headed?" asked an infantry officer who was eating an apple, also half smiling as he looked at the pretty girl.
The German closed his eyes, indicating he didn't understand.
"Here, take this if you'd like," said the officer, holding out the apple to the girl.

The girl smiled and took it. Nesvitsky, like every other man on the bridge, kept his eyes on the women until they had passed. When they were gone, the same stream of soldiers continued with the same kind of chatter, and finally everyone came to a halt. As so often happens, the horses pulling a supply wagon had balked at the end of the bridge, and the entire crowd was forced to wait.

"Why have they stopped? No order at all!" the soldiers grumbled. "Where do you think you're shoving? To hell with you! Can't you wait? It'll be even worse if he sets fire to the bridge. Look—there's an officer stuck too." Different voices in the crowd said these things as the men looked at one another and all pressed toward the far end of the bridge.
Looking down at the waters of the Enns beneath the bridge, Nesvitsky suddenly heard a new sound—something approaching fast, something large that splashed into the water.
"See where that one landed!" a soldier nearby said grimly, glancing around at the sound.
"Encouraging us to move faster," said another nervously.
The crowd surged forward again. Nesvitsky realized it had been a cannonball.
"Hey, Cossack! My horse!" he called. "Now then, make way! Get out of the way!"

With enormous difficulty he reached his horse, and shouting nonstop, he pushed forward. The soldiers squeezed aside to let him through but immediately pressed in on him again, jamming his leg. Those nearest him weren't to blame—they were being crushed from behind even harder.
"Nesvitsky! Nesvitsky, you blockhead!" came a hoarse voice from behind.

Nesvitsky turned and saw, about fifteen paces back but cut off by the solid, moving mass of infantry, Vaska Denisov—red-faced and shaggy, his cap shoved to the back of his black head, a cloak thrown dashingly over one shoulder.

"Tell these devils—these fiends—to let me through!" Denisov shouted, clearly in a fury, his coal-black eyes with their bloodshot whites glittering and rolling as he waved his sheathed saber in a small, bare hand as red as his face.
"Vaska!" Nesvitsky called back joyfully. "What's going on?"

"The squadwon can't get thwough!" Vaska Denisov shouted, baring his white teeth fiercely and spurring his black thoroughbred Arab, which flicked its ears as bayonets grazed it and snorted, spraying white foam from its bit, stamping the bridge planks with its hooves—looking ready to vault right over the railings if its rider allowed it. "What is this? They're like sheep! Just like sheep! Out of the way! Let us through! You there with the cart—I'll cut you down with my saber!" he yelled, actually drawing his saber and brandishing it.
The soldiers crushed against each other with terrified faces, and Denisov managed to reach Nesvitsky.
"How is it you're not drunk today?" Nesvitsky asked when Denisov had ridden up alongside.
"They don't even give you time to dwink!" Denisov answered. "They keep dwagging the wegiment back and forth all day. If we're going to fight, then let's fight. But God only knows what this is."
"What a dandy you look today!" said Nesvitsky, eyeing Denisov's new cloak and saddle cloth.
Denisov grinned, pulled a handkerchief from his sabretache that gave off a waft of perfume, and pressed it to Nesvitsky's nose.
"Of course! I'm going into action! I've shaved, bwushed my teeth, and put on cologne."

The imposing bulk of Nesvitsky, trailed by his Cossack, combined with Denisov's fierce determination as he swung his sword and shouted like a madman, had such an effect that they managed to force their way through to the far side of the bridge and halt the infantry. At the bridgehead, Nesvitsky found the colonel he needed to deliver the order to, and having done so, rode back.

Having cleared the way, Denisov stopped at the end of the bridge. Casually reining in his stallion—which was neighing and pawing the ground, eager to rejoin the other horses—he watched his squadron approaching. The clang of hooves, as if several horses were galloping at once, rang out on the bridge planks, and the squadron, officers in front and men four abreast, spread across the bridge and began emerging on his side.

The infantry soldiers who had been held up stood in the trampled mud near the bridge and watched with that particular mixture of hostility, detachment, and mockery that troops of different branches typically feel when they encounter one another—watching the clean, smart hussars ride past in neat formation.
"Pretty boys! Only good for a parade!" one said.
"What use are they? Just marched around for show!" another remarked.
"Don't kick up the dust, you foot-sloggers!" joked a hussar whose prancing horse had splattered mud on several infantrymen.

"I'd like to see you after a two-day march with a knapsack! Those fancy trousers would get worn through soon enough," said an infantryman, wiping mud off his face with his sleeve. "Sitting up there, you look more like a bird than a man."
"Hey, Zikin, they ought to put you on a horse. You'd be a sight!" said a corporal, teasing a scrawny little soldier bowed under the weight of his knapsack.
"Stick a branch between your legs—that'll do for your horse!" the hussar shouted back.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: The last of the infantry hurried across the bridge, bunching tighter as they neared it, as if squeezing through a funnel. Finally all the baggage wagons had crossed, the crowding eased, and the last battalion reached the bridge. Now only Denisov's squadron of hussars remained on the far side, facing the enemy. The French could be seen from the hill on the opposite bank but were not yet visible from the bridge itself, because the horizon as viewed from the river valley was formed by rising ground barely half a mile away. At the foot of the hill stretched wasteland where a few groups of Cossack scouts were moving about. Then suddenly, on the road at the top of the high ground, artillery and troops in blue uniforms appeared. These were the French. A group of Cossack scouts trotted back down the hill. All the officers and men of Denisov's squadron tried to talk about other things and look elsewhere, but every one of them was thinking only about what was up on that hilltop, and they kept glancing at the shapes appearing on the skyline—shapes they knew to be enemy troops. The weather had cleared again since midday, and the sun was sinking brightly over the Danube and the dark hills surrounding it. It was quiet, and at intervals the sound of bugle calls and shouting from the enemy drifted down from the hill. Between the squadron and the enemy there was now nothing but a handful of scattered skirmishers. An empty stretch of about seven hundred yards was all that separated them. The enemy had stopped firing, and that stern, menacing, untouchable line dividing two hostile armies could be felt more sharply than ever.

One step beyond that invisible boundary—which feels like the line between the living and the dead—lies uncertainty, suffering, and death. And what is over there? Who is over there? Beyond that field, that tree, that sunlit rooftop? No one knows, but you want to know. You are afraid to cross that line, and yet you long to cross it, knowing that sooner or later you must, and that you will have to discover what lies on the other side—just as you will inevitably have to learn what lies beyond death. But you are strong, healthy, cheerful, and keyed up, surrounded by others who are just as excited and alive. That is what anyone thinks, or at least feels, when they come within sight of the enemy, and that feeling lends a special intensity and joyful sharpness to everything that happens in such moments.

On the high ground where the enemy stood, a puff of cannon smoke rose and a ball came whistling over the heads of the hussar squadron. The officers who had been clustered together rode off to their positions. The hussars carefully straightened their formation. Silence fell over the entire squadron. Every man watched the enemy ahead and the squadron commander, waiting for the order. A second cannonball flew past, then a third. They were clearly aiming at the hussars, but each ball whistled rapidly overhead and landed somewhere beyond. The hussars didn't turn around, but at the sound of each shot—as if on command—the whole squadron, with its rows of faces so alike and yet so different, rose slightly in the stirrups, held its breath while the ball passed, and then settled back. Without turning their heads, the soldiers stole glances at each other, curious to read their comrades' reactions. On every face, from Denisov's down to the bugler's, the same expression showed around the chin and mouth: a mixture of tension, irritation, and excitement. The quartermaster glared at his men as though threatening punishment. Cadet Mironov flinched every time a ball flew past. Rostov, on the left flank astride his horse Rook—a handsome animal despite its lame leg—wore the happy look of a schoolboy called up for an exam before a large audience, confident he's going to shine. He kept glancing around with a bright, clear expression, as if inviting everyone to notice how calm he was under fire. But despite himself, that same hint of something new and serious showed around his mouth too.
"Who's ducking over there? Cadet Miwonov! That's not wight! Look at me!" Denisov called out. Unable to stay still, he kept wheeling his horse back and forth in front of the squadron.

The black, hairy, snub-nosed face of Vaska Denisov, and his whole short, sturdy frame with its sinewy hand and stubby fingers gripping the hilt of his bared saber, looked just as it always did—especially toward evening when he'd emptied his second bottle. He was only redder than usual. With his shaggy head thrown back the way birds do when they drink, pressing his spurs ruthlessly into the flanks of his good horse Bedouin, sitting as if he were falling backward in the saddle, he galloped to the other end of the squadron and shouted in a hoarse voice for the men to check their pistols. Then he rode up to Kirsten. The staff captain, on his broad-backed, steady mare, came toward him at a walk. His face with its long mustache was as serious as ever; only his eyes were brighter than usual.
"Well, what do you think?" Kirsten said to Denisov. "It won't come to a fight. Watch—we'll pull back."
"The devil only knows what they're up to!" Denisov muttered. "Ah, Wostov!" he cried, catching sight of the cadet's bright face. "You've finally got your chance!"
He smiled approvingly, clearly pleased with the young man. Rostov felt completely happy. Just then the commander appeared on the bridge. Denisov galloped up to him.
"Your excellency! Let us attack them! I'll dwive them off!"

"Attack, indeed!" the colonel said in a bored voice, scrunching his face as though swatting away a fly. "And why are you standing here? Can't you see the skirmishers are pulling back? Lead the squadron out."

The squadron crossed the bridge and moved out of range without losing a single man. The second squadron, which had been in the front line, followed them across, and the last Cossacks withdrew from the far bank.

The two Pavlograd squadrons, having crossed the bridge, retired up the hill one after the other. Their colonel, Karl Bogdanich Schubert, rode up to Denisov's squadron and proceeded at a walking pace near Rostov, without taking any notice of him—even though this was their first encounter since the incident with Telyanin. Rostov, feeling that he was at the front and in the power of a man toward whom he now admitted he'd been in the wrong, kept his eyes fixed on the colonel's athletic back, his light-haired nape, and his red neck. It struck Rostov that Bogdanich was only pretending not to notice him, and that his real purpose was to test the cadet's courage. So he straightened up and looked around cheerfully. Then it seemed to him that Bogdanich was riding so close on purpose, to show off his own bravery. Next he imagined that the colonel would send the squadron on some desperate charge just to punish him—Rostov. And then he pictured how, after the charge, Bogdanich would approach him as he lay wounded and magnanimously extend the hand of reconciliation.

The high-shouldered figure of Zherkov, familiar to the Pavlograds since he'd only recently left their regiment, rode up to the colonel. After being removed from headquarters, Zherkov hadn't stayed with the regiment, claiming he wasn't fool enough to toil at the front when he could earn more rewards by doing nothing on the staff. He had managed to attach himself as an orderly officer to Prince Bagration. Now he came to his former commander with an order from the rear guard.
"Colonel," he said, addressing Rostov's enemy with an air of solemn gravity, glancing around at his former comrades, "there's an order to halt and set fire to the bridge."
"An order from whom?" the colonel asked sourly.
"I don't exactly know 'from whom,'" the cornet replied in a serious tone, "but the prince told me: 'Go and tell the colonel that the hussars must return at once and burn the bridge.'"

Behind Zherkov came another officer from the suite, riding up to the hussar colonel with the same order. After him, the stout Nesvitsky came galloping up on a Cossack horse that could barely carry his weight.

"Colonel, what's going on?" he shouted as he approached. "I told you to set fire to the bridge, and now someone's gone and botched it. Everyone over there is in a panic and nobody can figure out what's happening."
The colonel deliberately halted the regiment and turned to Nesvitsky.
"You spoke to me about inflammable material," he said, "but you said nothing about setting fire to it."

"But my dear sir," said Nesvitsky, reining in and taking off his cap to smooth his sweat-dampened hair with his plump hand, "wasn't I telling you to burn the bridge after the inflammable material had been placed?"

"I am not your 'dear sir,' Mister Staff Officer, and you did not tell me to burn the bridge! I know my duty, and I make it my habit to follow orders strictly. You said the bridge would be burned—but who was supposed to burn it? I couldn't know that by divine inspiration!"
"It's always the same!" Nesvitsky said with a wave of his hand. "How did you end up here?" he asked, turning to Zherkov.
"Same errand. But you're soaking wet! Let me wring you out!"
"You were saying, Mister Staff Officer..." the colonel continued in an offended tone.
"Colonel," the officer from the suite cut in, "you need to move quickly, or the enemy will bring up their guns for grapeshot."
The colonel looked silently at the suite officer, then at the stout staff officer, then at Zherkov, and he frowned.
"I vill ze bridge fire," he announced in a solemn tone, as if to declare that despite all the aggravation he was enduring, he would still do the right thing.

Striking his horse with his long, muscular legs as though the animal were to blame for everything, the colonel rode forward and ordered Denisov's squadron—the second, in which Rostov was serving—to return to the bridge.
"There it is—just as I thought," Rostov said to himself. "He wants to test me!" His heart clenched and the blood rushed to his face. "Let him see whether I'm a coward!" he thought.

Once again, the grave expression the men had worn under fire settled over every bright face in the squadron. Rostov kept watching his enemy, the colonel, closely, searching his face for confirmation of his suspicions. But the colonel never once glanced at Rostov and looked just as he always did at the front—solemn and stern. Then came the word of command.
"Quick! Quick!" several voices repeated around him.

Sabers catching on bridles and spurs jingling, the hussars hastily dismounted, none of them quite sure what they were supposed to do. The men were crossing themselves. Rostov no longer looked at the colonel—there was no time. He was terrified of falling behind the others, so terrified that his heart seemed to stop. His hand shook as he handed his horse off to an orderly, and he felt the blood pound against his chest. Denisov rode past him, leaning back and shouting something. Rostov saw nothing but hussars running all around him, their spurs catching and sabers clanking.
"Stretchers!" someone shouted behind him.

Rostov didn't stop to think about what that call meant. He just ran, trying to stay ahead of everyone. But right at the bridge, not watching his feet, he stepped into some sticky, trampled mud, stumbled, and fell on his hands. The others rushed past him.
"At both sides, Captain," he heard the colonel's voice. Bogdanich had ridden ahead and pulled up his horse near the bridge, his face triumphant and cheerful.

Rostov wiped his muddy hands on his trousers, looked at his enemy, and was about to run forward again, thinking the further ahead he got, the better. But Bogdanich, without looking at him or showing any sign of recognition, shouted:
"Who's running down the middle of the bridge? To the right! Come back, Cadet!" he shouted angrily. Then, turning to Denisov, who had ridden out onto the bridge planks to show off his courage:
"Why take unnecessary risks, Captain? You should dismount," he said.
"Every bullet has its target," Vaska Denisov replied, turning in his saddle.

Meanwhile, Nesvitsky, Zherkov, and the officer from the suite stood together out of range, watching—now the small cluster of men in yellow shakos, dark-green braided jackets, and blue riding trousers swarming around the bridge, and now what was approaching from the far side: blue uniforms and groups of men with horses, clearly recognizable as artillery.

"Will they manage to burn the bridge or not? Who'll get there first? Will they set it ablaze, or will the French get close enough for grapeshot and wipe them out?" Every man watching from the high ground above the bridge was asking himself these questions with a sinking heart, gazing at the bridge and the hussars in the bright evening light and the blue-coated troops advancing from the other side with bayonets and guns.
"The hussars are going to catch it!" Nesvitsky said. "They're within grapeshot range now."
"He shouldn't have taken so many men," the officer from the suite remarked.
"That's true enough," Nesvitsky agreed. "Two quick fellows could have done the job just as well."

"Ah, your excellency," Zherkov put in, his eyes fixed on the hussars but still wearing that guileless look that made it impossible to tell whether he was joking or serious. "How you look at things! Send two men? But then who would earn the Vladimir medal and ribbon? As it is, even if they do get peppered, the squadron can be put up for honors and he can win a ribbon. Our Bogdanich knows how things are done."
"There!" said the officer from the suite. "That's grapeshot."
He pointed to the French guns, whose limbers were being hurriedly detached and pulled away.

On the French side, a cloud of smoke rose from one of the gun positions, then a second and a third almost simultaneously. At the moment the first report reached them, a fourth flash was visible. Then two booms in quick succession, and a third.
"Oh! Oh!" Nesvitsky groaned as if in sharp pain, grabbing the officer from the suite by the arm. "Look! A man's gone down! Down, down!"
"Two, I think."
"If I were Tsar, I would never go to war," Nesvitsky said, turning away.

The French guns were hastily reloaded. The infantry in blue advanced toward the bridge at a run. Smoke appeared again in irregular bursts, and grapeshot crackled and rattled against the bridge. But this time Nesvitsky couldn't see what was happening there—a dense cloud of smoke had risen from the bridge. The hussars had managed to set it on fire, and the French batteries were now shooting at them not to stop them, but simply because the guns were aimed and there were targets to hit.

The French managed to fire three rounds of grapeshot before the hussars made it back to their horses. Two of the rounds went wide, the shot sailing too high, but the last one landed in the middle of a cluster of hussars and knocked three of them down.

Rostov, preoccupied with his feelings about Bogdanich, had stopped on the bridge with no idea what to do. There was no one to cut down—he had always imagined battles with saber in hand—and he couldn't help burn the bridge since he hadn't brought any burning straw like the other soldiers. He just stood there looking around, when suddenly he heard a rattling sound on the bridge, like nuts being spilled, and the hussar nearest to him fell against the railing with a groan. Rostov rushed over with the others. Again someone shouted, "Stretchers!" Four men grabbed the hussar and began lifting him.
"Oh God! For Christ's sake, leave me alone!" the wounded man cried, but they lifted him anyway and placed him on the stretcher.

Nicholas Rostov turned away and gazed into the distance, as if searching for something—at the waters of the Danube, at the sky, at the sun. How beautiful the sky was: how blue, how calm, how deep! How bright and glorious the setting sun! How softly the distant waters of the Danube glittered! And more beautiful still were the far-off blue mountains beyond the river, the convent, the mysterious gorges, the pine forests veiled in mist at their summits... There was peace there, and happiness... "I would want nothing else, nothing at all, if only I were there," Rostov thought. "In me alone and in that sunshine there is so much happiness. But here... groans, suffering, fear, and this chaos and rush... Over there—they're shouting again, and again everyone is running somewhere, and I'll run with them, and it—death—is here, above me and all around me... One more instant, and I will never again see this sun, this water, that gorge!..."

At that moment the sun began to slip behind the clouds, and more stretchers came into view before Rostov. And the fear of death and of the stretchers, and the love of the sun and of life, all merged into a single feeling of nauseating dread.
"Oh Lord God! You who are in that heaven—save me, forgive me, and protect me!" Rostov whispered.
The hussars ran back to the men holding their horses. Their voices grew louder and calmer. The stretchers disappeared from sight.
"Well, fwiend? So you've had a taste of gunpowder!" Vaska Denisov shouted right above his ear.
"It's all over—but I'm a coward. Yes, a coward!" Rostov thought, and with a deep sigh he took Rook from the orderly—the horse was standing with one hoof resting—and began to mount.
"Was that grapeshot?" he asked Denisov.

"You bet it was!" Denisov cried. "You all worked like real heroes, and it's nasty business! A charge is good work—hacking away at the enemy! But this kind of thing is pure hell, with them shooting at you like you're a target."
Denisov rode up to a group that had gathered near Rostov, made up of the colonel, Nesvitsky, Zherkov, and the officer from the suite.
"Well, it seems no one noticed," Rostov thought. And it was true. No one had paid any attention, because everyone understood the sensation that a cadet experiences under fire for the first time.
"Here's something for you to report," said Zherkov. "Watch—I'll get promoted to sub-lieutenant for this."
"Inform ze prince zat I ze bridge fired!" the colonel declared, triumphant and beaming.
"And if he asks about the losses?"

"A trifle," the colonel said in his deep bass voice. "Two hussars wounded, and one knocked out." He couldn't hold back a satisfied smile, and he pronounced the words "knocked out" with ringing clarity.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Pursued by a French army of a hundred thousand men under Bonaparte's command, met by a hostile local population, losing faith in its allies, short of supplies, and forced to operate under conditions of war that no one had anticipated, the Russian army of thirty-five thousand under Kutuzov was retreating rapidly along the Danube. It halted when overtaken by the enemy and fought rearguard actions only as far as necessary to continue its retreat without losing its heavy equipment. There had been engagements at Lambach, Amstetten, and Melk, but despite the courage and endurance with which the Russians fought—acknowledged even by the enemy—the only result of these battles was an even faster retreat. The Austrian troops that had escaped capture at Ulm and joined Kutuzov at Braunau now broke away from the Russian army, leaving Kutuzov with nothing but his own weak and exhausted forces. The defense of Vienna was no longer thinkable. Instead of the offensive campaign whose plan, carefully devised according to the modern science of strategy, had been handed to Kutuzov in Vienna by the Austrian War Council, his sole remaining objective—and a nearly unattainable one—was to link up with the reinforcements marching from Russia without losing his army the way Mack had lost his at Ulm.

On October 28, Kutuzov crossed with his army to the left bank of the Danube and took up a position for the first time with the river between himself and the bulk of the French forces. On the thirtieth, he attacked Mortier's division on the left bank and shattered it. In this engagement, trophies were captured for the first time: banners, cannons, and two enemy generals. For the first time after two weeks of retreat, Russian troops had halted and, after a fight, had not only held the field but driven the French back. Though the troops were poorly clothed, exhausted, and had lost a third of their strength to dead, wounded, sick, and stragglers—though many of the sick and wounded had been left behind on the far side of the Danube with a letter entrusting them to the enemy's mercy—and though the large hospitals and houses in Krems that had been converted into military hospitals could no longer hold all the casualties—the stand at Krems and the victory over Mortier lifted the army's spirits considerably. Throughout the entire army and at headquarters, the most optimistic (though inaccurate) rumors were circulating: that Russian reinforcement columns were approaching, that the Austrians had won some victory, and that a frightened Bonaparte was in retreat.

Prince Andrew had served during the battle as aide to the Austrian General Schmidt, who was killed in the action. His horse had been shot from under him and a bullet had grazed his arm. As a mark of the commander in chief's special favor, he was chosen to carry the news of this victory to the Austrian court, which was now at Brünn rather than Vienna, since Vienna was threatened by the French. Despite his seemingly delicate build, Prince Andrew could endure physical hardship far better than many much stronger men. On the night of the battle, having arrived at Krems excited but not tired, with dispatches from Dokhturov for Kutuzov, he was immediately sent on with a special dispatch to Brünn. Being chosen for such a mission meant not only a reward but an important step toward promotion.

The night was dark but starry. The road showed black against the snow that had fallen the day before—the day of the battle. Replaying his impressions of the recent fight, pleasantly imagining the reaction his news of victory would produce, remembering the send-off from the commander in chief and his fellow officers, Prince Andrew raced along in a post chaise, savoring the feelings of a man who has finally begun to achieve a long-desired happiness. As soon as he closed his eyes, his ears filled with the rattle of wheels and the sensation of victory. Then he would start imagining that the Russians were fleeing and that he himself had been killed—but he quickly shook off the vision with a surge of joy, as if discovering all over again that none of it was true, that on the contrary, it was the French who had fled. He recalled every detail of the victory once more, and his own steady courage during the battle, and feeling reassured, he drifted off to sleep... The dark, starry night gave way to a bright, cheerful morning. The snow was melting in the sunshine, the horses galloped briskly, and on both sides of the road stretched forests of different kinds, fields, and villages.

At one of the relay stations he overtook a convoy of Russian wounded. The Russian officer in charge of the transport was sprawled in the front cart, shouting at a soldier with crude abuse. In each of the long German carts, six or more pale, dirty, bandaged men were being jolted over the rough road. Some were talking—he caught Russian words—and others were chewing bread. The more severely wounded watched in silence, with the dull curiosity of sick children, as the courier rushed past them.

Prince Andrew told his driver to stop and asked a soldier which battle they had been wounded in. "Day before yesterday, on the Danube," the soldier answered. Prince Andrew took out his purse and gave the man three gold coins.
"That's for all of them," he said to the officer who came up.
"Get well soon, lads!" he called to the soldiers. "There's still plenty to do."
"Any news, sir?" asked the officer, clearly eager to strike up a conversation.
"Good news! Drive on!" he shouted to his driver, and they galloped away.

It was already quite dark by the time Prince Andrew rattled over the cobblestone streets of Brünn and found himself surrounded by tall buildings, the glow of shop windows and house lamps, elegant carriages, and all the bustle of a large, lively city—always so appealing to a soldier after life in camp. Despite his rapid journey and sleepless night, he felt even more energized and alert as he pulled up to the palace than he had the day before. Only his eyes had a feverish gleam, and his thoughts followed one another with extraordinary speed and clarity. He relived the details of the battle once more—no longer hazy, but sharp and precise, framed in the concise form in which he imagined reporting them to Emperor Francis. He vividly anticipated the offhand questions that might be asked and the answers he would give. He expected to be ushered into the Emperor's presence immediately. At the main entrance to the palace, however, an official hurried out to meet him and, learning that he was a special messenger, directed him to a different entrance.
"To the right down the corridor, Your Excellency! There you'll find the adjutant on duty," the official said. "He will take you to the Minister of War."

The adjutant on duty met Prince Andrew, asked him to wait, and went in to see the minister. Five minutes later he returned and, bowing with exaggerated courtesy, led Prince Andrew along a corridor to the room where the Minister of War was working. The adjutant's elaborate politeness seemed designed to discourage any attempt at familiarity from the Russian messenger.

Prince Andrew's elated mood dimmed considerably as he approached the minister's door. He felt slighted, and without being fully aware of it, his sense of offense immediately hardened into a disdain that was entirely uncalled for. His quick mind instantly supplied a perspective that gave him the right to look down on both the adjutant and the minister. "Far from the smell of gunpowder, they probably think winning victories is easy!" he thought. His eyes narrowed scornfully as he entered the Minister of War's room with deliberately measured steps. This feeling of contempt only deepened when he saw the minister seated at a large table, reading documents and marking them with pencil notes, paying no attention whatsoever to his arrival for the first two or three minutes. A wax candle stood on either side of the minister's bent, bald head with its gray temples. He went on reading to the end without looking up at the sound of the door opening and footsteps approaching.
"Take this and deliver it," he said to his adjutant, handing over the papers and still not acknowledging the special messenger.

Prince Andrew felt that either Kutuzov's army interested the Minister of War less than the other matters on his desk, or the minister wanted to give that impression. "But it makes absolutely no difference to me," he thought. The minister gathered the remaining papers, straightened them into a neat pile, and finally raised his head. He had a distinctive, intelligent face—but the moment he turned to Prince Andrew, its firm, perceptive expression shifted in a way that was clearly deliberate and habitual. His face assumed the stupid, artificial smile—making no attempt whatsoever to disguise its falseness—of a man who spends his days receiving one petitioner after another.
"From Field Marshal Kutuzov?" he asked (in French). "Good news, I hope? An engagement with Mortier? A victory? It was about time!"
He took the dispatch addressed to him and began reading it with a sorrowful expression.
"Oh, my God! My God! Schmidt!" he exclaimed in German. "What a catastrophe! What a catastrophe!"
Having skimmed the dispatch, he laid it on the table and studied Prince Andrew, clearly turning something over in his mind.

"What a tragedy! You say the battle was decisive? But Mortier was not captured." He reflected again. "I'm very glad you've brought good news, though Schmidt's death is a heavy price for this victory. His Majesty will certainly want to see you, but not today. I thank you! You need rest. Come to the levee tomorrow, after the parade. I'll send word, however."
The stupid smile, which had vanished while he was speaking, reappeared on his face.
"Goodbye! Thank you very much. His Majesty will most likely wish to see you," he added (in French) with a bow.

When Prince Andrew left the palace, he felt that all the excitement and happiness the victory had given him had been surrendered into the indifferent hands of the Minister of War and the polite adjutant. The entire character of his thoughts changed in an instant; the battle now seemed like the memory of some distant event, long past.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Prince Andrew stayed in Brünn with Bilibin, a Russian he knew from the diplomatic service.

"Ah, my dear Prince! I couldn't ask for a more welcome guest," said Bilibin, coming out to meet Prince Andrew. "Franz, put the prince's things in my bedroom," he told the servant who was showing Bolkonski in. "So you're a bearer of victory news? Wonderful! And here I am sitting around sick, as you can see."
After washing and changing, Prince Andrew came into the diplomat's luxurious study and sat down to the dinner that had been prepared for him. Bilibin settled himself comfortably by the fire.

After his journey and the campaign, during which he'd been deprived of every comfort of cleanliness and refinement, Prince Andrew felt a pleasant sense of ease among the luxurious surroundings he'd been accustomed to since childhood. Beyond that, it was pleasant—after his reception by the Austrians—to speak, if not in Russian (they were speaking French), at least with a Russian who would, he assumed, share the general Russian hostility toward the Austrians that was particularly intense at the time.

Bilibin was a thirty-five-year-old bachelor who moved in the same circles as Prince Andrew. They'd known each other previously in Petersburg but had become closer when Prince Andrew was in Vienna with Kutuzov. Just as Prince Andrew was a young man who showed every sign of rising high in the military, so Bilibin—to an even greater extent—showed every sign of rising in the diplomatic world. He was still young but no longer a novice diplomat, having entered the service at sixteen and served in Paris and Copenhagen before landing a fairly important post in Vienna. Both the foreign minister and the Russian ambassador in Vienna knew him and valued him. He wasn't one of those many diplomats who are respected merely because they have certain negative qualities, avoid doing certain things, and speak French. He was one of those who genuinely enjoyed work and knew how to do it well, and despite his natural laziness would sometimes spend an entire night at his desk. He worked well regardless of the subject matter. It wasn't the question "What for?" but "How?" that interested him. He didn't particularly care what a diplomatic matter was about, but it gave him enormous pleasure to craft a circular, memorandum, or report with skill, precision, and elegance. Bilibin's services were valued not only for his writing but also for his ability to deal and converse with people in the highest spheres.

Bilibin enjoyed conversation the way he enjoyed work—only when it could be made elegantly witty. In society he was always waiting for a chance to say something memorable and only joined a conversation when such an opportunity arose. His talk was always laced with cleverly original, polished phrases of general interest. These sayings were prepared in the inner workshop of his mind in portable form, as if designed so that minor society figures could carry them from one drawing room to the next. And indeed, Bilibin's witticisms circulated through the Viennese salons and often had an influence on matters considered important.

His thin, worn, sallow face was covered with deep wrinkles that always looked as clean and well-scrubbed as fingertips after a long bath. The movement of these wrinkles was the principal means of expression on his face. His forehead would furrow into deep folds with his eyebrows raised, then his eyebrows would drop and deep creases would form on his cheeks. His small, deep-set eyes always sparkled and looked straight at you.
"Well, tell me about your exploits," he said.
Bolkonski, very modestly and without once mentioning himself, described the battle and his reception by the Minister of War.
"They received me and my news the way you'd receive a dog that wanders into a bowling alley," he concluded.
Bilibin smiled and the wrinkles on his face disappeared.

"However, my dear fellow," he remarked (in French), examining his nails from a distance and puckering the skin above his left eye, "despite the deep respect I hold for the Orthodox Russian army, I must confess that your victory was not exactly the most victorious of victories."
* Cependant, mon cher, malgré la haute estime que je professe pour the Orthodox Russian army, j'avoue que votre victoire n'est pas des plus victorieuses.
He went on talking this way in French, switching to Russian only for words he wanted to make contemptuous.
"Come now! You fell on the unfortunate Mortier with your entire force—his single division—and even then Mortier slipped through your fingers! Where's the victory in that?"
"But seriously," said Prince Andrew, "we can at least say without boasting that it was somewhat better than Ulm..."
"Why didn't you capture even one marshal for us?"

"Because things don't always go according to plan or unfold with parade-ground precision. We expected, as I told you, to reach their rear by seven in the morning but didn't get there until five in the afternoon."
"And why didn't you get there at seven in the morning? You should have been there by seven," returned Bilibin with a smile. "You should have been there at seven in the morning."
"Why didn't you manage to convince Bonaparte through diplomatic channels to leave Genoa alone?" retorted Prince Andrew in the same tone.

"I know," interrupted Bilibin, "you're thinking it's very easy to capture marshals while sitting on a sofa by the fire! That's true enough, but still—why didn't you capture him? So don't be surprised if not only the Minister of War but also His Most August Majesty Emperor and King Francis isn't exactly thrilled by your victory. Even I, a lowly secretary of the Russian Embassy, feel no need to celebrate by giving my Franz a coin or letting him go off to the Prater with his sweetheart... Though of course, we don't have a Prater here."
He looked Prince Andrew straight in the eye and suddenly smoothed his forehead.

"Now it's my turn to ask you 'why?' my dear fellow," said Bolkonski. "I confess I don't understand—perhaps there are diplomatic subtleties here beyond my humble intelligence—but I can't make sense of it. Mack loses an entire army, Archduke Ferdinand and Archduke Karl show no signs of life and blunder after blunder. Kutuzov alone wins a real victory, breaking the spell of French invincibility, and the Minister of War doesn't even want to hear the details."

"That's exactly the point, my dear fellow. You see, it's all 'hurrah for the Tsar, for Russia, for the Orthodox faith!' That's all very well, but what do we—I mean the Austrian court—care about your victories? Bring us good news of a victory by Archduke Karl or Ferdinand—one archduke's as good as another, as you know—even if it's only over a fire brigade of Bonaparte's, and that would be another story entirely: we'd fire off cannons! But this kind of thing seems designed to annoy us. Archduke Karl does nothing, Archduke Ferdinand disgraces himself. You abandon Vienna, give up its defense—as if to say: 'God is with us, but you and your capital are on your own!' The one general we all loved—Schmidt—you get killed by a bullet, and then you congratulate us on the victory! Admit it: more irritating news than yours could hardly be imagined. It's as though it were done on purpose, completely on purpose. Besides, suppose you did win a brilliant victory—even if Archduke Karl had won one—what difference would it make to the overall course of events? It's too late now that Vienna is occupied by the French army!"
"What? Occupied? Vienna occupied?"
"Not only occupied—Bonaparte is at Schönbrunn, and the count, our dear Count Vrbna, goes to him for his orders."
After the exhaustion of the journey, his reception, and especially after dinner, Bolkonski found he could not fully grasp the significance of what he was hearing.

"Count Lichtenfels was here this morning," Bilibin continued, "and showed me a letter describing the French parade through Vienna in full detail: Prince Murat and the whole spectacle... So you see, your victory is hardly cause for celebration, and you can't expect to be received as a savior."

"Honestly, I don't care about that. I really don't care at all," said Prince Andrew, beginning to realize that his news of the battle near Krems was truly insignificant compared to something like the fall of Austria's capital. "But how was Vienna taken? What about the bridge and its famous fortifications? What about Prince Auersperg? We'd heard that Prince Auersperg was defending Vienna."

"Prince Auersperg is on this side of the river—our side—and he's defending us. Doing it rather badly, I'd say, but still defending us. Vienna, though, is on the other side. No, the bridge hasn't been taken yet, and I hope it won't be, since it's been mined and orders have been given to blow it up. Otherwise we'd have long since been in the Bohemian mountains, and you and your army would have had a very bad time caught between two fires."
"But this still doesn't mean the campaign is over," said Prince Andrew.

"Well, I think it is. The big men here think so too, but they don't dare say it. It will be as I said at the start of the campaign: it won't be your skirmish at Dürrenstein, or gunpowder at all, that decides this—but the people who planned it," said Bilibin, quoting one of his own bon mots, releasing the wrinkles on his forehead, and pausing. "The only question now is what comes of the meeting between Emperor Alexander and the King of Prussia in Berlin. If Prussia joins the allies, Austria's hand will be forced and there will be war. If not, it's just a matter of deciding where to draw up the terms of the new Campo Formio."
"What an extraordinary genius!" Prince Andrew suddenly exclaimed, clenching his small fist and striking the table. "And what luck the man has!"

"Bonaparte?" said Bilibin inquiringly, wrinkling his forehead to signal that a witticism was coming. "Buonaparte?" he repeated, stressing the 'u.' "I think, however, now that he's laying down the law for Austria at Schönbrunn, il faut lui faire grâce de l'u! — we really must drop the 'u.' I shall certainly adopt the innovation and simply call him Bonaparte!"
* "We must let him off the u!"
"But joking aside," said Prince Andrew, "do you really think the campaign is over?"

"Here's what I think. Austria has been made a fool of, and she's not used to it. She'll retaliate. And she's been made a fool of in the first place because her provinces have been pillaged—they say the holy Russian army loots terribly—her army is destroyed, her capital taken, and all this for the sake of His Sardinian Majesty's lovely eyes. And therefore—this is just between us—I have an instinctive feeling that we're being deceived. My instinct tells me there are negotiations with France going on, and plans for peace—a secret, separate peace."
* beaux yeux
"Impossible!" cried Prince Andrew. "That would be too despicable."
"If we live, we'll see," replied Bilibin, his face becoming smooth again—a sign the conversation was over.

When Prince Andrew reached the room prepared for him and lay down in a clean shirt on the feather bed with its warm, fragrant pillows, he felt that the battle whose news he'd brought was far, far away from him. The alliance with Prussia, Austria's treachery, Bonaparte's latest triumph, tomorrow's levee and parade, and his audience with Emperor Francis occupied his thoughts.

He closed his eyes, and immediately a roar of cannon fire, musketry, and the rattling of carriage wheels seemed to fill his ears, and once again in his mind the musketeers were descending the hill in a thin line, the French were firing, and he felt his heart pounding as he rode forward beside Schmidt with bullets whistling cheerfully all around. He experienced the joy of being alive tenfold, as he hadn't since childhood.
He woke up...
"Yes, all of that really happened!" he said, and smiling to himself like a happy child, he fell into a deep, youthful sleep.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The next day he woke late. As his recent impressions came flooding back, the first thought in his mind was that today he had to be presented to Emperor Francis. He remembered the Minister of War, the courteous Austrian adjutant, Bilibin, and last night's conversation. Having dressed in full parade uniform—which he hadn't worn in a long time—he went into Bilibin's study looking fresh, lively, and handsome, with his hand still bandaged. Four gentlemen from the diplomatic corps were already in the study. Prince Andrew was already acquainted with Prince Hippolyte Kuragin, who served as a secretary to the embassy. Bilibin introduced him to the others.

The gentlemen gathered at Bilibin's were young, wealthy, fashionable men who formed a special circle both here and in Vienna. Bilibin, their leader, called the group "ours." This set, made up almost entirely of diplomats, clearly had its own interests that had nothing to do with war or politics but revolved around high society, certain women, and the ceremonial side of government service. These gentlemen welcomed Prince Andrew as one of their own—an honor they extended to very few. Out of politeness, and to start a conversation, they asked him a few questions about the army and the battle, but then the talk quickly turned to lighthearted jokes and gossip.
* les nôtres

"But the best part was," said one, telling the story of a fellow diplomat's misfortune, "that the Chancellor told him point-blank that his posting to London was a promotion and that he should treat it as such. Can you imagine the look on his face?"
"But the worst of it, gentlemen—and I'm giving Kuragin away here—is that the man is genuinely suffering, and this Don Juan, this scoundrel, is taking advantage of it!"
Prince Hippolyte was sprawled in a lounge chair with his legs thrown over the armrest. He started laughing.
"Tell me about that!" he said.
"Oh, you Don Juan! You snake!" cried several voices.

"You don't know this yet, Bolkonski," said Bilibin, turning to Prince Andrew, "but all the horrors committed by the French army—I almost said the Russian army—are nothing compared to what this man has been doing to the women here!"
"Woman is man's companion," announced Prince Hippolyte (in French), peering through a lorgnette at his own elevated legs.
* La femme est la compagne de l'homme.

Bilibin and the rest of "ours" burst out laughing right in Hippolyte's face, and Prince Andrew saw that Hippolyte—of whom, he had to admit, he had nearly been jealous on his wife's account—was the group's favorite target.
"Oh, I have to give you a treat," Bilibin whispered to Bolkonski. "Kuragin is priceless when he talks politics—you have to see how serious he gets!"
He sat down next to Hippolyte, furrowed his brow, and began talking to him about politics. Prince Andrew and the others gathered around the two of them.

"The Berlin cabinet cannot express a sentiment of alliance," Hippolyte began (in French), looking around importantly at the others, "without expressing... as in its last note... you understand... Besides, unless His Majesty the Emperor departs from the principle of our alliance..."

"Wait, I'm not finished..." he said to Prince Andrew, grabbing him by the arm. "I believe that intervention will prove stronger than non-intervention. And..." He paused. "Finally, one cannot attribute the non-receipt of our dispatch of November eighteenth. That is how it will end." And he released Bolkonski's arm to show he had quite finished.
"Demosthenes, I recognize you by the pebble hidden in your golden mouth!" said Bilibin, and the tuft of hair on his head bobbed with satisfaction.
Everyone laughed, and Hippolyte louder than anyone. He was clearly embarrassed and breathing hard, but he couldn't contain the wild laughter that contorted his normally blank features.

"Well then, gentlemen," said Bilibin, "Bolkonski is my guest here in this house and in Brünn itself. I want to show him the best time I can, with all the pleasures life here has to offer. If we were in Vienna it would be easy, but here in this miserable Moravian backwater it's harder, and I'm asking all of you to help me. You can handle the theater, I'll take care of society, and you, Hippolyte—the women, naturally."
"We absolutely must introduce him to Amelie—she's divine!" said one of "ours," kissing his fingertips.
"In general, we need to convert this bloodthirsty soldier to more civilized pursuits," said Bilibin.
"I'm afraid I won't be able to take advantage of your hospitality, gentlemen. It's already time for me to go," replied Prince Andrew, glancing at his watch.
"Where to?"
"To see the Emperor."
"Oh! Oh! Oh!"
"Well, goodbye, Bolkonski! Goodbye, Prince! Come back early for dinner," called several voices. "We'll look after you."
"When you're speaking with the Emperor, try to say good things about the supply situation and the route planning," said Bilibin, walking him to the hall.
"I'd like to speak well of them, but as far as I know the facts, I can't," replied Bolkonski with a smile.
"Well, talk as much as you can anyway. He has a passion for giving audiences, but he doesn't like talking himself and can't manage it, as you'll see."

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: At the levee, Prince Andrew stood among the Austrian officers as instructed, and Emperor Francis merely stared fixedly at his face and gave a slight nod with his long head. But after it was over, the adjutant he'd seen the day before ceremoniously informed Bolkonski that the Emperor wished to grant him an audience. Emperor Francis received him standing in the middle of the room. Before the conversation began, Prince Andrew was struck by the fact that the Emperor seemed flustered and kept blushing, as if he didn't know what to say.
"Tell me, when did the battle begin?" he asked hastily.

Prince Andrew answered. Then came more questions, equally straightforward: "Was Kutuzov in good health? When had he left Krems?" The Emperor spoke as though his only goal were to get through a set number of questions—the answers, quite obviously, didn't interest him.
"At what time did the battle begin?" the Emperor asked.

"I cannot inform Your Majesty at what time the battle began at the front lines, but at Dürrenstein, where I was stationed, our attack began after five in the afternoon," replied Bolkonski, growing more animated and expecting he might finally have the chance to give a reliable account—which he had prepared in his mind—of all he knew and had seen. But the Emperor smiled and cut him off.
"How many miles?"
"From where to where, Your Majesty?"
"From Dürrenstein to Krems."
"Three and a half miles, Your Majesty."
"The French have abandoned the left bank?"
"According to the scouts, the last of them crossed on rafts during the night."
"Is there sufficient forage in Krems?"
"Forage has not been supplied to the extent—"
The Emperor cut him off.
"At what time was General Schmidt killed?"
"At seven o'clock, I believe."
"At seven o'clock? That is very sad, very sad!"

The Emperor thanked Prince Andrew and bowed. Prince Andrew withdrew and was immediately surrounded on all sides by courtiers. Everywhere he saw friendly faces and heard kind words. Yesterday's adjutant reproached him for not having stayed at the palace and offered him the use of his own house. The Minister of War came up to congratulate him on the Order of Maria Theresa, third class, which the Emperor was bestowing on him. The Empress's chamberlain invited him to see Her Majesty. The archduchess also wished to see him. He didn't know whom to respond to first and took a few seconds to collect his thoughts. Then the Russian ambassador took him by the shoulder, led him to the window, and began talking.

Contrary to Bilibin's prediction, the news Prince Andrew had brought was received with joy. A thanksgiving service was arranged, Kutuzov was awarded the Grand Cross of Maria Theresa, and the entire army received decorations. Bolkonski was invited everywhere and had to spend the whole morning making calls on the leading Austrian dignitaries. Between four and five in the afternoon, having completed all his calls, he was walking back to Bilibin's house, composing in his head a letter to his father about the battle and his visit to Brünn. At the door he found a carriage half-loaded with luggage. Franz, Bilibin's servant, was struggling to drag a heavy trunk out through the front door.
Before returning to Bilibin's, Prince Andrew had stopped at a bookshop to stock up on books for the campaign and had spent some time browsing.
"What's going on?" he asked.
"Oh, Your Excellency!" said Franz, wrestling the trunk toward the carriage. "We have to move on again. That scoundrel is at our heels!"
"What? What do you mean?" asked Prince Andrew.
Bilibin came out to meet him. His usually calm face showed excitement.
"There now! You have to admit this is delightful," he said. "The Thabor Bridge affair, in Vienna... They've crossed it without firing a shot!"
Prince Andrew couldn't grasp what he meant.
"Where have you been that you don't know what every cab driver in town knows?"
"I've been at the archduchess's. I heard nothing there."
"And you didn't notice that everyone is packing up?"
"I didn't... What's this all about?" Prince Andrew asked impatiently.

"What's it about? The French have crossed the bridge that Auersperg was supposed to be defending, and the bridge was not blown up. So now Murat is racing down the road toward Brünn and will be here in a day or two."
"What? Here? But why didn't they blow up the bridge if it was mined?"
"That's exactly what I'd like to know. Nobody—not even Bonaparte himself—can explain it."
Bolkonski shrugged.
"But if the bridge has been crossed, it means the army is lost too. It'll be cut off," he said.

"That's precisely the situation," answered Bilibin. "Listen. The French entered Vienna as I told you. Fine. The next day—which was yesterday—these gentlemen, the marshals Murat, Lannes, and Belliard, mount their horses and ride to the bridge. (Note that all three are Gascons.) 'Gentlemen,' says one of them, 'you know the Thabor Bridge is mined and double-mined, that there are serious fortifications at the bridgehead, and that fifteen thousand men have orders to blow it up and keep us from crossing. But it would please our sovereign Emperor Napoleon if we took this bridge, so let's go take it!' 'Yes, let's!' say the others. And off they go and take the bridge, cross it, and now their entire army is on this side of the Danube, marching toward us—toward you, and your supply lines."
* messieurs les maréchaux
"Stop joking," said Prince Andrew, sadly and seriously. The news pained him, and yet at the same time he was pleased.

The moment he learned that the Russian army was in such a desperate position, it occurred to him that he was the one destined to lead it out of this crisis—that here was the Toulon that would lift him from the ranks of obscure officers and offer him his first step toward glory! As he listened to Bilibin, he was already imagining how, upon reaching the army, he would present an opinion at the war council—the only plan that could save them—and how he alone would be entrusted with carrying it out.
"Stop the joking," he said.

"I'm not joking," Bilibin went on. "Nothing could be more true or more tragic. These gentlemen ride onto the bridge alone, waving white handkerchiefs. They assure the officer on duty that they, the marshals, are on their way to negotiate with Prince Auersperg. He lets them into the bridgehead. They spin a thousand tall tales, saying the war is over, that Emperor Francis is arranging a meeting with Bonaparte, that they'd like to see Prince Auersperg, and so on. The officer sends for Auersperg. The gentlemen embrace the Austrian officers, crack jokes, sit on the cannons, and meanwhile a French battalion slips onto the bridge unnoticed, throws the detonation charges into the water, and reaches the fortifications. At last the lieutenant general himself appears—our dear Prince Auersperg von Mautern. 'Dearest enemy! Flower of the Austrian army! Hero of the Turkish wars! Hostilities are over, we can shake hands... Emperor Napoleon burns with impatience to make Prince Auersperg's acquaintance.' In short, these gentlemen—true Gascons—so bewildered him with their fine words, and he was so flattered by his sudden intimacy with the French marshals, and so dazzled by the sight of Murat's cloak and ostrich plumes, that he couldn't see what was right in front of him—and forgot he was supposed to be firing on the enemy!" Despite his animated delivery, Bilibin didn't forget to pause after this bon mot to let it land. "The French battalion rushes the bridgehead, spikes the guns, and the bridge is taken! But the best part," he continued, his excitement subsiding under the pleasant momentum of his own story, "is that the sergeant in charge of the cannon—the one meant to give the signal to detonate the mines—seeing the French troops swarming onto the bridge, was about to fire. But Lannes grabbed his hand. The sergeant, who was clearly smarter than his general, went up to Auersperg and said: 'Prince, you're being deceived—these are the French!' Murat, seeing that all was lost if the sergeant was allowed to speak, turned to Auersperg with a look of feigned astonishment—a true Gascon—and said: 'I hardly recognize the world-famous Austrian discipline when you allow a subordinate to address you like that!' It was a stroke of genius. Prince Auersperg, feeling his authority challenged, ordered the sergeant arrested. Come on, you have to admit this Thabor Bridge business is magnificent! It's not exactly stupidity, and it's not exactly treachery either..."
* tête-de-pont
* qu'il n'y voit que du feu, et oublie celui qu'il devait faire faire sur l'ennemi!
"It might be treachery," said Prince Andrew, vividly picturing the gray overcoats, the wounds, the gunpowder smoke, the sounds of battle, and the glory that awaited him.

"Not that either. That would put the court in too bad a light," replied Bilibin. "It's not treachery, not villainy, not stupidity—it's just like Ulm... it's..." He seemed to be searching for the right expression. "It's... it's a case of Mack. We've been Macked," he concluded, feeling he had produced a fresh witticism that would make the rounds. His previously furrowed brow smoothed out with pleasure, and with a slight smile he began examining his nails.
"Where are you off to?" he said suddenly to Prince Andrew, who had risen and was heading toward his room.
"I'm leaving."
"Where?"
"To the army."
"But you were planning to stay two more days."
"Now I'm leaving at once."
And Prince Andrew, after giving instructions for his departure, went to his room.
"You know, my dear fellow," said Bilibin, following him, "I've been thinking about you. Why are you going?"
And as proof of the finality of his opinion, all the wrinkles vanished from his face.
Prince Andrew looked at him questioningly and said nothing.
"Why are you going? I know you think it's your duty to gallop back to the army now that it's in danger. I understand. My dear fellow, it is heroism!"
"Not at all," said Prince Andrew.

"But as a philosopher, be a consistent one. Look at the other side of the question and you'll see that your duty is actually to take care of yourself. Leave the heroics to those who are no longer fit for anything else... You haven't been ordered to return, and you haven't been dismissed from here. So you can stay and go wherever our bad luck takes us. They say we're heading for Olmütz, and Olmütz is a perfectly decent town. You and I will travel comfortably in my carriage."
"Stop joking, Bilibin," said Bolkonski.

"I'm speaking sincerely, as a friend! Think about it. Where are you going, and why, when you could stay here? You're facing one of two outcomes"—and the skin over his left temple puckered—"either you won't reach your regiment before peace is concluded, or you'll share in the defeat and disgrace of Kutuzov's entire army."
And Bilibin smoothed his temple, feeling his dilemma was unanswerable.
"I can't argue about it," replied Prince Andrew coldly, though he was thinking: "I am going to save the army."
"My dear fellow, you are a hero!" said Bilibin.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: That same night, after taking leave of the Minister of War, Bolkonski set off to rejoin the army, not knowing where he would find it and fearing he might be captured by the French on the way to Krems.

In Brünn, everyone connected to the court was packing up, and the heavy baggage had already been dispatched to Olmütz. Near Hetzelsdorf, Prince Andrew reached the main road along which the Russian army was moving at great speed and in complete disorder. The road was so clogged with wagons that it was impossible to get through in a carriage. Prince Andrew got a horse and a Cossack escort from a Cossack commander, and hungry and exhausted, threading his way past the baggage wagons, he rode in search of the commander in chief and his own luggage. The most alarming reports about the army's situation reached him as he went, and the sight of the troops in their chaotic retreat confirmed every rumor.

He remembered words from Bonaparte's address to his army at the beginning of the campaign: "That Russian army which English gold has transported from the ends of the earth—we shall make it share the same fate as the army at Ulm." (in French) These words awakened in him astonishment at his hero's genius, a sting of wounded pride, and a hope for glory. "And if all that's left is to die?" he thought. "Well, if it comes to that, I'll do it no worse than anyone else."
* Cette armée russe que l'or de l'Angleterre a transportée des extrémités de l'univers, nous allons lui faire éprouver le même sort—(le sort de l'armée d'Ulm).

He looked with contempt at the endless, chaotic mass of detachments, wagons, guns, artillery pieces, and still more baggage trains and vehicles of every kind, overtaking one another and blocking the muddy road three and sometimes four abreast. From all sides, in front and behind, as far as the ear could reach, came the rattle of wheels, the creaking of carts and gun carriages, the tramp of horses, the crack of whips, shouts, cursing from soldiers and orderlies and officers urging their horses on. Along both sides of the road lay fallen horses—some skinned, some not—and broken-down carts beside which solitary soldiers sat waiting for something. Other soldiers, breaking away from their units in groups, headed off to the nearby villages or returned from them dragging sheep, chickens, hay, and bulging sacks. On every uphill and downhill stretch the crowds grew denser and the shouting more frantic. Soldiers, sinking knee-deep in mud, pushed the guns and wagons with their own hands. Whips cracked, hooves slipped, harness straps snapped, and lungs were strained with shouting. The officers directing the march rode back and forth between the wagons. Their voices were barely audible over the uproar, and you could see from their faces that they had given up any hope of restoring order.
"Here's our beloved Orthodox Russian army," thought Bolkonski, remembering Bilibin's words.

Wanting to find out where the commander in chief was, he rode up to a convoy. Coming straight toward him was a strange one-horse vehicle, obviously cobbled together by soldiers from whatever materials they could find—something between a cart, a buggy, and a carriage. A soldier was driving it, and behind the leather hood sat a woman wrapped in shawls. Prince Andrew rode up and was about to ask a soldier for directions when he was interrupted by the desperate screaming of the woman in the vehicle. An officer in charge of the transport column was beating the soldier who drove the woman's cart for trying to push ahead of the others, and his whip was landing on the vehicle's canvas cover. The woman shrieked piercingly. Seeing Prince Andrew, she leaned out from behind the cover and, waving her thin arms from beneath a woolen shawl, cried:

"Aide-de-camp! Aide-de-camp! For God's sake... protect me! What will become of us? I'm the wife of the doctor of the Seventh Chasseurs... They won't let us through, we've been left behind and lost our people..."
"I'll flatten you like a pancake!" shouted the angry officer at the soldier. "Turn back with your woman!"
"Aide-de-camp! Help me! What is happening?" screamed the doctor's wife.
"Let this cart through. Can't you see it's a woman?" said Prince Andrew, riding up to the officer.
The officer glanced at him, and without answering turned back to the soldier. "I'll teach you to push ahead!... Back!"
"Let them through, I said!" repeated Prince Andrew, his lips pressed tight.

"And who are you?" shouted the officer, turning on him in a state of drunken rage. "Who are you? Are you in command here? Eh? I'm in command here, not you! Get back or I'll flatten you like a pancake!" he repeated. The expression clearly pleased him.
"That was a nice put-down for the little aide-de-camp," came a voice from behind.

Prince Andrew saw that the officer was in that state of blind, drunken fury when a man doesn't know what he's saying. He realized that defending the doctor's wife in her ramshackle cart might expose him to what he dreaded more than anything in the world—ridicule. But his instinct drove him forward. Before the officer could finish his sentence, Prince Andrew, his face twisted with fury, rode straight at him and raised his riding whip.
"Let—them—through!"
The officer flung his arm in the air and hastily rode away.
"It's all the fault of these headquarters people—they're the ones causing this chaos," he muttered. "Do what you want."

Prince Andrew, without looking up, rode quickly away from the doctor's wife, who was calling him her savior. Recalling every detail of the humiliating scene with disgust, he galloped on to the village where he'd been told the commander in chief was located.

Reaching the village, he dismounted and went to the nearest house, hoping to rest even for a moment, eat something, and try to sort out the painful, tormenting thoughts swirling in his mind. "This isn't an army—it's a mob of scoundrels," he thought as he approached the window of the first house, when a familiar voice called out his name.
He turned around. Nesvitsky's handsome face was looking out of a small window. Nesvitsky, chewing something and moving his moist lips, was waving his arm and calling him over.
"Bolkonski! Bolkonski! Can't you hear me? Come here, quickly!" he shouted.

Going inside, Prince Andrew found Nesvitsky and another adjutant eating. They spun around to face him, asking if he had any news. On their familiar faces he read alarm and anxiety. This was especially striking on Nesvitsky's face, which was usually so cheerful.
"Where is the commander in chief?" asked Bolkonski.
"Here, in that house," answered the adjutant.
"Well, is it true? Peace and surrender?" asked Nesvitsky.
"I was going to ask you. I know nothing except that I barely managed to get here."
"And us, my dear fellow! It's terrible! I was wrong to laugh at Mack—we're getting it even worse," said Nesvitsky. "But sit down and have something to eat."
"You won't be able to find your baggage or anything else now, Prince. And God only knows where your man Peter is," said the other adjutant.
"Where is headquarters?"
"We're spending the night in Znaim."

"Well, I've managed to pack everything I need onto two horses," said Nesvitsky. "They made up excellent packs for me—good enough to cross the Bohemian mountains. Things look grim, old friend!
